TITLE: Provably-Unbiased KernelSHAP for Ordinal Features
PROPOSAL: We extend the work of unbiased KernelSHAP by incorporating a weighted encoding scheme that maps ordinal features to a high-dimensional Euclidean space. Specifically, we represent each feature as a binary vector where the number of ones reflects the magnitude of the feature value. This mapping enables unbiased KernelSHAP to account for the ordinal structure of features, providing a more accurate estimate of Shapley values. We provide a theoretical analysis of this extension in terms of its convergence rate and bias-variance tradeoff.
CONTROLS: Standard KernelSHAP without ordinal encoding as a baseline for comparison
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: By incorporating ordinal encoding, Provably-Unbiased KernelSHAP for Ordinal Features (PUK) should demonstrate improved accuracy and convergence rate for estimating Shapley values on real-world datasets with ordinal features, especially in high-dimensional spaces where correlations and interdependencies between features are prominent. However, its adaptability to non-ordinal categorical features might lead to decreased performance compared to standard KernelSHAP.

TITLE: LeverageSHAP vs KernelSHAP on Tabular Datasets with Feature Correlations
PROPOSAL: We compare the performance of LeverageSHAP and KernelSHAP on a range of tabular datasets, focusing on their ability to accurately estimate Shapley values in the presence of feature correlations and interdependencies. We measure the accuracy of both estimators using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE) and KL-divergence. To analyze the impact of feature correlations, we intentionally construct datasets with varying levels of interdependencies between features.
CONTROLS: Standard KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP without specializations or modifications as a baseline for comparison, as well as the Provably-Unbiased KernelSHAP for Ordinal Features (PUK) for a nuanced comparison of KernelSHAP variants
COST: 3300
PREDICTION: LeverageSHAP likely outperforms KernelSHAP in terms of accuracy, particularly in datasets with strong feature correlations, due to its adaptive sampling strategy that leverages statistical leverage scores. However, the performance of KernelSHAP might be improved by its recent extension with ordinal encoding, such as PUK, which specializes the architecture to capture ordinal feature relationships. Nevertheless, the comparative advantage of LeverageSHAP might still outweigh the (moderate) improvements seen with the KernelSHAP specializations in numerous scenarios.

TITLE: SHAP-Ensemble: A Hybrid Model for Improving Shapley Value Estimations using Ensemble Methods
PROPOSAL: We introduce SHAP-Ensemble, a novel approach that combines multiple Shapley value estimators using ensemble methods to improve the accuracy and reliability of feature importance scores. By leveraging the strengths of different estimation techniques, SHAP-Ensemble aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of model behavior and feature contributions.
CONTROLS: Existing Shapley value estimators, including KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP, and the proposed efficient inference for long-tailed Shapley values, as well as ablations of the SHAP-Ensemble framework
COST: 20000

However, the additional complexity and computational requirements of SHAP-Ensemble may lead to decreased performance in scenarios with limited computational resources.

TITLE: Investigating Temporal Attention in Multimodal Transformers for Temporal Change Description
PROPOSAL: We experiment with different attention mechanisms for temporally ordering the sequence of satellite images when using a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) for temporal change description. Specifically, we compare (1) a standard self-attention mechanism, (2) a hierarchical temporal attention mechanism that captures both short-term and long-term temporal relationships, and (3) an Inter-Predictor Attention mechanism inspired by ubiquitous learning, where the model adaptively selects the most relevant contextual information to reason about each change. Our hypothesis is that hierarchical or adaptive attention can improve accuracy in capturing long-range temporal dynamics and underlying causal narratives of changes.
CONTROLS: We will compare these variants against the standard MLLM baseline and ablate the use of temporal attention by training on sequences with randomly permuted temporal orderings.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical temporal attention mechanism to achieve state-of-the-art results for temporal change description, with the Inter-Predictor Attention following closely behind. If successful, this would demonstrate the importance of designing temporal attention mechanisms for effective long-range temporal understanding.

TITLE: Land-Use Change-Centric Prompt Engineering for Improved Forecasting Accuracy
PROPOSAL: We examine how leveraging domain-specific knowledge about land-use change dynamics through prompt engineering can enhance the accuracy of future satellite image forecasting. By incorporating a diverse set of informative prompts, tailored to specific types of change (e.g., urbanization, deforestation, agricultural expansion), we condition the MLLM to reason about the spatial and temporal properties of change patterns that have been historically observed. Specifically, we investigate whether prompts that highlight the causal relationships, spatial coherence, and temporal continuance of changes lead to improved forecasting accuracy compared to generic or scenario-based prompts.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against a baseline that uses generic scene description prompts and against the MLLM without prompt engineering for change-heavy regions.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Enhancing the MLLM with land-use change-specific prompts significantly improves forecasting accuracy for regions with high change rates, especially in accurately modeling causal and spatial relationships of land-use changes. Performance is predicted to decrease as change rates are depleted.

By constructing a graph representing the causal relationships between spatially distributed features, such as land-use patterns, water bodies, and infrastructure, we enable the model to reason about why changes occur over time. The causal graph is continuously updated and refined during training using temporal embeddings derived from satellite image time series data. We use this causal graph as an auxiliary input to the MLLM, guiding its reasoning and decision-making process for forecasting future changes.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach with standard MLLM-based forecasting and evaluate its performance on various metrics, such as MAE and temporal consistency.

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Temporal Consistency Metrics on Forecasting Evaluation
PROPOSAL: We propose a study to investigate the effectiveness of various temporal consistency metrics in evaluating the quality of forecasts generated by our models. We will design a set of metrics that assess the degree of temporal consistency in forecasts, including metrics that measure the spatial coherence of changes, the temporal logical progression of changes, and the overall match between forecasted and actual changes over time. We will then evaluate the performance of our models using these metrics, as well as standard metrics such as MAE and RMSE, to gain insights into the strengths and weaknesses of our approaches.

TITLE: Investigating the Role of Transfer Learning in Satellite Image Time Series Models
PROPOSAL: We explore the potential benefits of transfer learning in satellite image time series models, where a pre-trained model is fine-tuned on a new, related task. We will investigate whether models pre-trained on large-scale satellite image datasets can be adapted to new areas of interest, such as land-use change monitoring or agricultural cycle forecasting, with minimal additional training. We will also examine how transfer learning can be used to leverage knowledge from one region to improve forecasting performance in another region, taking into account factors such as climate, topography, and human activity.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of transfer-learned models against models trained from scratch on each new task, as well as against each other, to evaluate the benefits and limitations of transfer learning in this context.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Our study is expected to show that transfer learning can significantly improve the performance of satellite image time series models, especially for tasks that share common characteristics or geographic regions, by leveraging pre-existing knowledge and adapting it to new scenarios.

TITLE: Reevaluating update components in OGD for time series forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the standard update components, i.e., final-layer weights or adapters attached to a model's input or output, are indeed optimal under distribution shift for time series forecasting. Instead, we propose to update mid-level representations within the pre-trained model, as these might retain the spatial relationships between features captured by convolutional or recurrent layers. We hypothesize that adapting these representations will lead to more robust forecasts when data patterns change.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard approach of updating final-layer weights; ablating the adapter module; keeping the base model frozen and the adapter module updated.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect a modest performance gain from updating mid-level representations under moderate distribution shift; however, if the adapters are not sufficiently reinitialized, we may see similar performance as standard OGD.

TITLE: Adaptive dead-time compensation in OGD for multi-step forecasting
PROPOSAL: In multi-step forecasting, the delayed feedback from future values causes lag in gradient-based updates. To address this issue, we introduce an adaptive dead-time compensation mechanism in OGD. This involves keeping a running estimate of the delay-induced error and adding it to the loss function, in effect, accelerating the update process. We hypothesize that this mechanism will enable more reliable and robust adaptation in environments with delayed feedback.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard OGD without dead-time compensation; ablating the dead-time compensation module to assess its contribution.
COST: 1728
PREDICTION: We expect that the adaptive dead-time compensation mechanism will reduce the lag-induced performance degradation and lead to notable improvements in forecast accuracy, especially in the long-term forecasts. However, if the delay in feedback is highly variable and unpredictable, the adaptation mechanism may not compensate effectively for the dead time.

TITLE: Self-calibrating forgetting mechanisms for online adaptation
PROPOSAL: A major challenge in online adaptation is forgetting learned patterns and adjusting to changing conditions. Inspired by theories of synaptic pruning in neuroscience, we propose a self-calibrating forgetting mechanism that gradually eliminates parameters with the smallest update norms, aiming to stabilize the adaptation process. The forgetting rate will be dynamically adjusted based on the model's performance on recent data, facilitating adaptation to evolving patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard OGD; compare with an implementation where the forgetting rate is fixed rather than self-calibrating.
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: We expect that our self-calibrating forgetting mechanism will enable more stable and efficient adaptation to changing conditions, especially in scenarios with significant concept drift. However, the model may still fail to adapt quickly enough to abrupt changes or out-of-distribution data.

TITLE: Diversity-driven ensemble of OGD variants for robust online forecasting
PROPOSAL: To reduce the risk of overfitting to a specific realization of OGD, we propose a diversity-driven ensemble method. The ensemble consists of multiple variants of OGD, each adapting distinct subsets of parameters, using different forgetting mechanisms, or incorporating various quantities of delayed feedback. The ensemble combines the predictions from each variant using weights learned through a meta-learning process, promoting a diverse set of models that specialize in adapting to different patterns in the data.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard OGD; compare the ensemble method with an ablation where the variants differ only in the parameters updated (as opposed to a more comprehensive search of OGD variants).
COST: 2916
PREDICTION: We expect that the diversity-driven ensemble will provide more robust and accurate forecasts, especially when faced with sudden changes or out-of-distribution data. However, if the ensemble becomes too complex or the meta-learning process fails to find a good set of weights, performance may degrade instead.

TITLE: Normalization-aware online adaptation for distribution shift
PROPOSAL: To mitigate the effects of distribution shift, we propose integrating normalization-aware online adaptation into the OGD framework. Specifically, we adapt the normalization parameters (e.g., mean and variance) in parallel with the model's weights, using a separate set of gradients computed from the normalized input. We also explore how to efficiently update the normalization parameters, taking into account the batch normalization paradigm where the moving average is updated with a decay rate.
CONTROLS: Compare with the standard OGD approach; compare with an ablation where normalization parameters are fixed or updated independently without being aware of the model's weights adaptation.
COST: 3400
PREDICTION: We expect that normalization-aware online adaptation will provide better handling of distribution shift, facilitate robustness against concept drift, and improve overall forecasting accuracy in time series data. However, if normalization statistics adaptation interacts negatively with self-calibrating forgetting, we might need to balance their effects or rethink the order of weight adaptation and normalization update.

PROPOSAL: To make the normalization-aware online adaptation more tractable, we explore parameterizing the normalization statistics in a tangent space instead of directly adjusting them. This formulation enables more efficient updates with reduced computational overhead and provides a more stationary behavior of the normalization statistics. We also investigate using a conformal transformation in the tangent space for the normalization parameters adaptation to further stabilize this process and improve adaptability to changing conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard OGD; compare with the previous normalization-aware online adaptation implementation; compare with an ablation where normalization parameters are updated using a different approach in the tangent space or a conformal transformation.

PREDICTION: We expect that tangent space parameterization will improve the robustness and accuracy of the normalization-aware online adaptation approach, especially against sudden changes in input data. However, non-trivial settings or complex normalization regimes may cause difficulties in the parameter estimation and stabilization in the tangent space.

TITLE: Multitask learning for devising effective update strategies in OGD
PROPOSAL: We propose a multitask learning approach to devise effective update strategies for OGD. Specifically, we train a neural meta-learner jointly on multiple tasks (update strategies), each corresponding to adapting different aspects of the pre-trained model (e.g., weight decay, learning rates, parameter subsets). The meta-learner learns a universal updater that can adapt to changing environments, ensuring improved robustness and scalability against various types of distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard OGD; compare with different variants of the multitask learning setup, such as the type and formulation of tasks, and learning objectives.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect that the multitask learning approach will open up new possibilities for customization of update strategies in OGD, yielding better performance and generalization in real-world scenarios. However, training such neural meta-learners might be time-consuming and prone to overfitting if many update strategies are required.

TITLE: Learning to update with temporally-aware, generative models of time series data
PROPOSAL: We propose leveraging recent advancements in temporal generative modeling to learn effective update strategies for OGD that capture complex temporal relationships within time series data. Specifically, we train a generative model (e.g., conditional diffusion model) to model the sequential dependencies in the data and use it to inform the update process in OGD. This approach could adapt the model to varying patterns and improve performance under concept drift.

However, the model training process can be computationally expensive and may require large datasets for effective learning.
